article.title: California Mushrooms
article.author: Britta Hedlund
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. If you live in California, you've probably watched mushrooms pop up overnight in your yard after the first good rain. Maybe you spotted something bright orange on a trail, or a perfect white cap growing near an oak tree and thought — what is that thing? California's wet winters (roughly November through March) create ideal conditions for fungi. Whether you're in San Diego, the Bay Area, or somewhere in between, these are 20 species you're most likely to run into. If you want a second opinion in the field, try MushDex mushroom identifier — a free mushroom identification tool you can use online or through its mobile app. One thing before we dive in: never eat a wild mushroom based solely on an online article. Always confirm your ID with an experienced forager or your local mycological society. The Dangerous Ones and Common Lawn Mushrooms 1. Death Cap ( Amanita phalloides ) This is the one that keeps toxicologists up at night. Responsible for most fatal mushroom poisonings worldwide, it's established across California — especially under coast live oaks from the Bay Area northward. The cap ranges from olive-green to yellowish, and there's a sac-like volva at the base of the stem. If you remember only one mushroom on this list, make it this one. 2. Western Destroying Angel ( Amanita ocreata ) Southern California's most dangerous mushroom. It's all white, elegant, and fruits under oaks from late winter into spring. People mistake it for edible species constantly. If you find a pure white mushroom growing near oaks anywhere from San Diego to Santa Barbara — just walk away. 3. Fly Agaric ( Amanita muscaria ) The classic fairy-tale mushroom: bright red cap dotted with white warts. You'll see it under pines and in landscaped areas statewide. Toxic, yes, but so distinctive you're unlikely to confuse it with anything edible. Still makes a great photo. 4. Green-spored Parasol ( Chlorophyllum molybdites ) The number-one cause of mushroom poisoning in North America, and it loves Southern California lawns. Large, white, and often growing in fairy rings on grass. The giveaway? Its spore print comes out green. You'll see these pop up in San Diego and LA backyards after rain. 5. Yellow Stainer ( Agaricus xanthodermus ) This one looks a lot like the button mushrooms at the grocery store. The trick: scratch the cap or cut the base, and it turns bright chrome yellow and smells like ink. Very common in SoCal gardens and parks, and a frequent cause of nausea. 6. Common Fieldcap ( Agrocybe pediades ) Those small, tan, button-shaped mushrooms dotting your lawn after rain? Probably these. They're one of the most common lawn mushrooms in California. Not edible, and despite what you might read online — they're not psychedelic. Just a plain little lawn mushroom doing its thing. 7. Mower's Mushroom ( Panaeolina foenisecii ) Another tiny brown lawn mushroom you'll see everywhere. It gets confused with psychedelic species because of its size and color, but it isn't one. You'll mow right over hundreds of these every season. 8. Fairy Ring Mushroom ( Marasmius oreades ) Ever noticed dark green circles in a lawn with small tan mushrooms growing along the ring? That's a fairy ring, and these are actually edible — they're popular in European cooking. The catch: they grow alongside toxic look-alikes like certain Clitocybe species, so this isn't a beginner pick. 9. Yellow Houseplant Mushroom ( Leucocoprinus birnbaumii ) If a bright lemon-yellow mushroom appeared in your potted plant, this is probably it. Common in nursery soil and indoor pots year-round. Mildly toxic, so keep curious kids and pets away, but it's harmless to the plant itself — it's just feeding on organic matter in the potting mix. 10. Shaggy Mane ( Coprinus comatus ) Tall, white, and shaggy, these pop up along roadsides, in backyards, and on disturbed soil across the state. The cool part? Within hours of maturing, the cap dissolves into black ink. Edible when young and firm, but you have to cook them fast before they self-digest. One of the easiest mushrooms in California to recognize. Wood-Lovers, Edibles, and the Rest of the Crew If you're just getting started with foraging and want to practice identifying species before heading out, mushroom-identification.com is a free online tool that can help you build confidence. 11. Common Ink Cap ( Coprinopsis atramentaria ) Similar to the Shaggy Mane — grayish, and it dissolves into ink too. Here's the important part: if you eat this mushroom and drink alcohol within a couple of days, you'll get violently sick. It contains a compound that blocks alcohol metabolism. Technically edible, but most people skip it for obvious reasons. 12. Dyeball ( Pisolithus arhizus ) That weird, dark, lumpy blob at the base of your eucalyptus tree? Probably a Dyeball. Super common in Southern California, especially in sandy or poor soil. Not edible, but it's actually a beneficial fungus helping your tree absorb nutrients underground. 13. Western Jack-o'-Lantern ( Omphalotus olivascens ) A gorgeous orange mushroom growing in clusters at the base of oaks. It actually glows faintly in the dark. Unfortunately, it's toxic and gets mistaken for chanterelles. The key difference: Jack-o'-Lanterns have true gills and grow on wood, while chanterelles have blunt ridges and grow from soil. 14. Chicken of the Woods ( Laetiporus gilbertsonii ) Bright orange-and-yellow shelves growing on tree trunks — you can't miss it. One of California's most popular edible mushrooms, and beginners love it because nothing else really looks like it. One caveat: specimens growing on eucalyptus can cause stomach trouble for some people. 15. California Golden Chanterelle ( Cantharellus californicus ) The crown jewel of California foraging. Golden-yellow, funnel-shaped, and fruiting under oaks from December through March. These can get surprisingly large — some weigh over two pounds. Found across the state, including parts of Southern California. Just make sure you know the Jack-o'-Lantern comparison (#13) before picking. 16. Black Trumpet ( Craterellus calicornucopioides ) Dark gray to black, thin, and trumpet-shaped. Almost invisible against the forest floor — foragers call them "the horn of plenty" because once you spot one, you realize you've been standing on dozens. Mostly found in Northern California under oaks and tanoaks. Delicious, with a deep, smoky flavor. 17. King Bolete ( Boletus edulis var. grandedulis ) California's version of the famous porcini. Big brown cap, thick stem, spongy pores underneath instead of gills. Look for it in Northern California coastal pine forests in fall. If you find one in good shape before the bugs do, you've hit the foraging jackpot. 18. Candy Cap ( Lactarius rubidus ) A small, orange-brown mushroom that smells exactly like maple syrup when dried. People bake them into cookies, churn them into ice cream, and fold them into pancake batter. Found under oaks and conifers in Northern California during winter. One of the most unique edible mushrooms you'll find anywhere. 19. Morel ( Morchella spp.) That honeycomb-looking mushroom selling for $40 a pound at the farmers market? That's a morel. In California, your best bet is burned areas in the Sierra Nevada the spring after a wildfire. Unmistakable once you've seen one, but watch out for the false morel ( Gyromitra ), which has a wrinkled, brain-like cap instead of clean pits. 20. Turkey Tail ( Trametes versicolor ) Thin, leathery, fan-shaped brackets with beautiful concentric color bands in brown, tan, and white. You'll find them on dead logs and stumps everywhere in California, year-round. Not a culinary mushroom, but one of the most heavily researched fungi in the world — and one of the prettiest things you'll spot on a fallen log. Keep Going These 20 barely scratch the surface of what's out there. If you want to go deeper, connecting with your local mycological society — like the San Diego Mycological Society or the Bay Area Mycological Society — is the single best move you can make. One afternoon on a group foray will teach you more than months of reading. Happy mushrooming — and when in doubt, don't eat it.
